title: Duterte to enter plea on first day of trial
summary: Former president Rodrigo Duterte will be asked to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on the first day of his crimes against humanity trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Nov. 30.
byline: Pia Lee-Brago, Neil Jayson Servallos, Janvic Mateo

blocks.text: November 28, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Former president Rodrigo Duterte will be asked to enter a plea of guilty or not guilty on the first day of his crimes against humanity trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Nov. 30.
The landmark trial will start at 10 a.m. in The Hague (5 p.m. Manila time) with the reading of the charges against the 81-year-old former leader, who is required to attend his trial in person.
In accordance with the court’s practice, only the details of the three counts of crimes against humanity charges will be read to Duterte, instead of the 56 incidents underlying each count.

“Thereafter, the Chamber shall satisfy itself that the Accused understands the nature of the charges and afford him an opportunity to make an admission of guilt in accordance with Article 65 of the Statute or to plead not guilty,” read the second directions on the conduct of the proceedings released by the ICC Trial Chamber III on Thursday.

Duterte is facing charges over killings allegedly committed by the so-called Davao death squad while he was mayor or vice mayor of Davao City from 2013 to 2016, the alleged murders of high-value targets from 2016 to 2017 and the alleged murders and attempted murders in relation to barangay operations from 2016 to 2018.

To prove that the killings were part of a “systematic” and “widespread” attack against a civilian population, the required threshold for crimes against humanity, the ICC prosecutor will present evidence on 56 separate incidents involving around 85 murders and two attempted murders.
After Duterte enters his plea, the trial will proceed with the opening statements of the parties.
Although it was initially given up to six hours for its opening statement, the prosecution said it will only use two hours and 15 minutes.
The common legal representatives of the victims will have one hour and 15 minutes, while the defense will provide an outline of its case in the next hour.
“Thereafter, the Chamber will immediately commence with the testimony of the first prosecution witness,” it said.
The prosecution is expected to present five witnesses, either in person or via video link, during trial dates from Nov. 30 to Dec. 15.
Hearings will be conducted from Monday to Friday, with the sitting schedule as follows: 10 a.m. to 11 a.m., 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., 1:30 p.m. to 2:30 p.m. and 3 p.m. to 4 p.m.
The schedule was adopted to accommodate Duterte’s age and physical condition. He was earlier found fit to stand trial, based on the assessment of an independent panel of medical experts.
Except for closed or private sessions, the trial will be livestreamed on the ICC website and other online platforms. It will have a 30-minute delay.
According to the latest directions from the trial chamber, the trial will resume on Jan. 12 until Feb. 19. There will be no hearings from Feb. 22 to 26.
The next evidentiary block will be from March 1 to 24, then from April 5 to 30.
Imee, Robin file resolution

Meanwhile, opposition Sens. Imee Marcos and Robinhood Padilla have filed a resolution urging the Marcos administration to immediately stop all cooperation with the ICC, secure the release and repatriation of Duterte and halt efforts to enforce a reported arrest warrant against Sen. Ronald dela Rosa.

In pushing for a reassessment of the government’s stance, the senators cited the Philippines’ formal withdrawal from the Rome Statute, which took effect on March 17, 2019, and a Nov. 19, 2026 joint Heads of State Declaration toward Peace issued by US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

According to the resolution, the joint declaration by the three permanent members of the United Nations Security Council expressly recognized “that the principles of state consent and respect for the immunities of state officials are of paramount importance, and declaring that the ICC and similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction.”
Victims of violence don’t report to police

Monica Juma, executive director of the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime, noted the recent findings of a joint UNODC-United Nations Development Program-Office, which revealed that more than half of victims of violence never report their situations to the police or other competent authorities.

“Victims must be able to obtain assistance, protection and effective remedies, irrespective of their circumstances or social position, particularly those who experience discrimination, stigma or exclusion,” she said.
